chunk_findings.detail:
`last_activity` returns `0.0` for "no evidence of work" (missing/unreadable tree, failed `git status`, failed `git log`) and `last_commit_at` also returns `0.0` whenever `base` or `branch` is falsy (`if not (base and branch): return 0.0`). `0.0` is not a neutral sentinel in this API: it is epoch 1970-01-01, i.e. an *infinitely old* watermark. The caller described in the same diff (`services.leasebreak`, keyed off `idle_max_s`/`hold_max_s`) is expected to compare `now - watermark` against those thresholds, so any of these inputs makes an otherwise live lease look tens of years idle and therefore yield-requested and then breakable — and because `break_on_timeout` defaults to `True`, a waiter's ordinary `ddflow claim` breaks the holder's lane without anyone deciding.

Concrete repro: an item is leased and its holder is actively committing, but the recorded worktree path does not exist yet (or `G.status`/`G.run` returns a failure and yields `None`), so `last_activity` returns `0.0`; equally, a repo where the default base branch cannot be resolved makes `last_commit_at` return `0.0`, and a clean worktree makes `last_change_at` return `0.0`, so `max(0.0, 0.0) == 0.0` even though commits are landing on the branch. In both cases `now - 0.0 > hold_max_s` is true and the lease is broken, contradicting the stated goal that "a lease that shows progress never is" broken and that an unreadable tree must "never [be] an error". The module needs to distinguish "unknown" from "activity at t=0" (e.g. return `None`/`-1` and let the caller ignore the signal or fall back to the lease start time) rather than publishing `0.0` as a timestamp.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/treeactivity.py — `last_activity` / `last_commit_at`

chunk_findings.detail: The function's docstring specifies the notices come back "newest first", but the body builds a plain dict keyed by subject while iterating `events` in log order and then returns `list(out.values())` — i.e. insertion order, which is oldest break first. Overwriting `out[e.subject]` on a later break does not move the key to the end either, so an item that is broken, reclaimed and broken again still sorts at the position of its *first* break. Concrete case: an agent's lease on `a` is broken at 10:00 and on `b` at 11:00; `broken_notices(events, agent)` returns `[a(...), b(...)]`, and any consumer that renders only the head of the list (brief/heartbeat showing "the latest break") shows the 10:00 break and hides the newer 11:00 one. A `sorted(..., key=lambda n: -n["idle_s"])` or a reversed materialisation is needed to match the documented order; as written the ordering guarantee is simply not implemented.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leasebreak.py:broken_notices (`return list(out.values())`)

chunk_findings.detail: `_break_idle` breaks leases one at a time inside the `while clash:` loop and commits each break (`log.append("lease.expired", ...)`, `_remote_drop`, parking the holder per DX-park-and-resume) before it looks at the *next* clash. If a later clashing lease is judged not breakable while `asked`/`break_on_timeout` is in effect, the function raises `LeaseError` (or `return clash` when not asked) **after** already having broken and parked the earlier holder — the enclosing `claim` then fails, so the waiter's claim never lands and the waiter's merge the amendment names as the restore condition never happens. Concrete input: item `Z` owns globs `g1` and `g2`; `g1` overlaps an idle lease by agent A (past `idle_max_s`/`hold_max_s`) and `g2` overlaps an active lease by agent B. `ddflow claim --break Z` breaks A (A's lane is parked, `lease.expired` written for A's item), recomputes `glob_clash`, finds B, `judge` returns not breakable, and raises `LeaseError`. `Z` is never claimed, yet A is now parked with restore condition "Z's merge", which can never occur — A stays parked indefinitely. The same happens with `break_on_timeout` and no `--break`. The break should be evaluated for all clashes (or rolled back) before any break is committed, so a claim that ultimately refuses does not park another holder.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases.py:443-460 (_break_idle)

chunk_findings.detail: The shipped default `new = "true"` makes every plain `ddflow claim` auto-break a lease that is past `hold_max_s` with a stale watermark. The intent specifies the holder's lane is taken over only when the *waiter* explicitly asks ("it is breakable by the waiter with `ddflow claim --break`"), i.e. the break is supposed to be a deliberate, attributable act by the item that is recorded as waiting (DX-lease-wait-cycle). With this default the `--break` flag and the recorded-wait gating are inert on the default path: any agent claiming an unrelated item whose globs overlap (agent C) runs `ddflow claim <other>`, hits A's stale held lease, and silently parks A's lane and takes the globs without ever passing `--break` or being the waiter. Given the existing rationale that "forcing past a dependency or live lease lets two agents write one file," turning that on by default is the failure mode, not an additive nicety. If auto-break is really wanted it must default `false` (opt-in per project/org per the conformance requirement), so the explicit `--break` path stays the norm.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/upgrade/unreleased/knob_added.lease.break_on_timeout.toml

chunk_findings.detail: The two timeouts are independent user-settable knobs with no stated invariant that `idle_max_s < hold_max_s`. The feature's semantics require that ordering: at `idle_max_s` the holder is *asked* to yield and only at `hold_max_s` (later) does the lease become breakable, which is why the defaults are 900/3600. A project that overrides only one of them — e.g. sets `hold_max_s = 600` while `idle_max_s` stays at 900 — produces a lease that is breakable at 600s while it was never reported yield-requested; the holder gets no request in its next `ddflow` call before its lane is parked, exactly the silent-takeover the change is meant to prevent. The knob files (and the CLI/MCP/prompt surfaces the conformance item requires) need to reject or clamp `hold_max_s <= idle_max_s`.

chunk_findings.detail: The added help text for `lease.hold_max_s` states that when a contended, idle lease is broken "The holder keeps its branch and worktree and re-claims normally." This directly contradicts the change's own AMENDED design note: breaking a lease PARKS the holder's lane (DX-park-and-resume) — "worktree, branch and recorded gates are kept, the restore condition is the waiter's merge, and the holder is restored first when it clears." The help text still describes the pre-amendment mechanism ("gets the contested globs back only through the normal claim"). Concretely: if a waiter runs `ddflow claim --break` (or `break_on_timeout` fires automatically) against a holder that is mid-work, this user-facing contract tells the holder/coordinator that the holder must re-race a normal claim, whereas the decided behavior is that the lane is parked and restored *first* once the waiter's merge clears it. Since this `.ambr` is the golden snapshot of the emitted help, either the shipped behavior matches the text (and the amended park/restore-first requirement is unimplemented) or the shipped behavior parks the lane (and the golden text is wrong) — in both cases the change is inconsistent with its stated design. Fix by documenting the park/restore-first behavior here instead of "re-claims normally".
chunk_findings.title: tests/golden/__snapshots__/test_golden_outputs.ambr (new `lease.hold_max_s` help entry)

chunk_findings.detail: The test asserts that a plain `ddflow claim T2 --no-worktree` (no `--break`) returns 0 and prints `BROKE T1`, and `test_break_flag_is_required_when_break_on_timeout_is_off` shows this is only because `lease.break_on_timeout` defaults to true. The intent specifies the breaking mechanism as "after hold_max_s it is breakable by the waiter with `ddflow claim --break`" — an explicit act by the waiter, after the lease has been *marked yield-requested* and seen in brief/doctor/status. Under the behavior these tests lock in, any waiter that simply re-runs the ordinary `ddflow claim` (the exact retry loop that produced the code-3 refusal in the first place) breaks the holder's lease and parks its lane the instant `hold_max_s` passes, bypassing the yield-request/visibility step entirely. Either the implementation must require `--break` by default (in which case this test fails) or the change deviates from the stated design; the tests also bake in a new boolean knob (`lease.break_on_timeout`) that appears nowhere in the intent.

chunk_findings.detail: `_setup` sets both `lease.idle_max_s` and `lease.hold_max_s` to 1 second and claims T1, and the very next statement requires B's claim of T2 to be refused with code 3. That refusal is only correct if less than one second of wall time elapses between A's `claim T1` subprocess and B's `claim T2` subprocess. On a loaded CI host where the interpreter start-up plus event-log read/write of the second CLI invocation exceeds 1 s, T1 is already past both limits, so this claim takes the break path, returns 0, and the assertion `[0] == 3` fails (and the `broken`-event assertions downstream see a different event count). A threshold below the cost of a subprocess round-trip is a race, not a deterministic check.

chunk_findings.detail: The intent requires the lease to be "marked yield-requested in brief/doctor/status" and (3) that "the holder sees the request in its next ddflow call", and the AMENDED clause requires that breaking PARKS the holder's lane (worktree, branch and recorded gates kept, restore condition = waiter's merge, holder restored first). The tests only assert the `LB.judge` verdict object, `BROKE T1` text, `expired_at`, and one `broken_by` event; nothing exercises any reporting surface before the break, and nothing asserts that the parked lane's worktree/branch/gates survive or that the deferred restore happens (DX-park-and-resume). The mandated regression test — "an idle lease with a waiter is *reported* yield-requested and then breakable" — is therefore only half delivered, which conflicts with the hard constraint that ddflow rules "must have regression test" [D-rules-hierarchy].

chunk_findings.detail: The new `lease.hold_max_s` doc states that after a break "The holder keeps its branch and worktree and re-claims normally." That is the pre-amendment wording, and it contradicts the decision recorded in the very same change: the AMENDED 2026-10-15 note (DX-park-and-resume) says breaking PARKS the holder's lane — "worktree, branch and recorded gates are kept, the restore condition is the waiter's merge, and the holder is restored first when it clears." With the documented behaviour there is no parked lane and no restore-first guarantee: once the waiter merges and the globs free up, the holder must win an ordinary claim against whoever asks next, so a third agent can take the contested globs while the broken holder still has unmerged work on its branch — exactly the loss the amendment was written to prevent (the original text it echoes, "the holder gets the contested globs back only through the normal claim", was superseded). The knob's documented contract is therefore stale with respect to the change's own decided semantics; the yield-request is likewise only documented "in the holder's heartbeat and in brief", while the decision names brief/doctor/status, so `ddflow doctor` and `ddflow status` are documented as not showing it.

chunk_findings.detail: The new help text for `lease.hold_max_s` states that when a breakable lease is broken "the holder keeps its branch and worktree and re-claims normally". The change's own amended specification (AMENDED 2026-10-15, DX-park-and-resume) says breaking a lease PARKS the holder's lane: the worktree, branch and recorded gates are kept, the restore condition is the waiter's merge, and the holder is restored first when it clears. So the user-facing text describes the pre-amendment behaviour. Concretely: an agent whose lease was broken runs `ddflow config --explain` (this transcript's command), reads that it "re-claims normally", and immediately runs `ddflow claim` for its globs, instead of waiting to be restored when the waiter's merge clears — the opposite of the parking contract the rest of the change implements.

chunk_findings.detail: The declared behaviour of the yield-request mark is narrowed to "the holder's heartbeat and in brief", whereas the item requires the lease "marked yield-requested in brief/doctor/status". A yield-requested contention is therefore not promised in `ddflow doctor` or `ddflow status`, which are exactly the surfaces an operator watches when agents sit on a hot file — the 45-minute stall this change exists to make visible. Input: an idle contended lease past `idle_max_s`; a person running `ddflow status` or `ddflow doctor` is given no such mark by what this help text commits to.

chunk_findings.detail: The new knob documentation defines progress more narrowly than the change's own intent, and the defaults turn that narrower definition into a broken lease for an actively-working agent. The intent for this change states the progress watermark is "the last event that is not a lease renewal (a commit, a gate record, a **test job start**, a note)", but the `lease.idle_max_s` doc added here lists progress as only "a commit, a gate outcome, a note or any other event on the item, or a changed file in its worktree". A gate that is *running* (started, not yet recorded) is therefore not progress, and a `note`/`changed file` may not exist during a long gate. Concrete failure: `[ci].timeout_s` defaults to 3600 and the ci/unit_tests gate legitimately runs the whole suite for up to an hour; an agent that claims `src/foo.py`, runs `ddflow gate run ci`, and produces no commit, note, or gate *outcome* for `idle_max_s` (900 s) is falsely reported yield-requested, and at `hold_max_s` (3600 s) — reachable inside a single default-timeout gate — the lease becomes breakable, and with `lease.break_on_timeout = true` (default) a competing claim breaks it with no operator in the loop. That directly contradicts the regression criterion the change is supposed to satisfy ("an active lease never is [breakable]"): the holder is mid-gate, its lease is broken, and when it later commits the pre-commit path finds its globs no longer covered. Fix by including gate *starts* / long-running-job starts in the watermark (as the intent specifies) before `hold_max_s` can ever fire.

chunk_findings.detail:
`last_change_at` derives "progress" only from the mtime of files that still exist on disk: every status entry whose path cannot be `stat`ed is dropped (`except OSError: continue`), so a deletion contributes nothing to the watermark. But a deletion is exactly the kind of "changed file in its worktree" the feature defines as progress, and `last_activity` is the max of this and `last_commit_at`, so for a deletion-only edit the result collapses to the branch's commit time (or 0.0).

Concrete failure: agent A holds a contended lease acquired at t=0 on a lane whose newest commit unique to `base..branch` is older than `hold_max_s` (default 3600 s), or which has no unique commit at all. At t=3590 A runs `git rm legacy/*.py` (status shows `D  legacy/...`; `os.stat(tree/"legacy/x.py")` raises `FileNotFoundError`, `continue`), so no new timestamp is produced. The waiter's claim at t=3600 sees `last_activity` = the old commit time / 0.0, concludes A has been idle for `hold_max_s`, and breaks the lease — even though A changed the tree 10 s earlier. That contradicts the change's own regression criterion "an active lease never is [breakable]" and the config doc's promise that a "changed file in its worktree" counts as progress. A `git status`-based signal must consider index/worktree deletions (e.g., fall back to the index/entry type, or to the mtime of the containing directory) rather than requiring a surviving file.

chunk_findings.detail: The docstring promises the notices "newest first", but the function builds a dict and returns `list(out.values())` without any sort. Dict insertion order is the order in which each item's *first* break was seen, so for the normal chronological event stream the list is oldest-first. Input: item A broken at t=100 and item C broken at t=200, events fed in time order. `out["A"]` is inserted first, `out["C"]` second; the returned list is `[A notice, C notice]` — the holder's most recent (and most actionable) break is shown last, contradicting the documented ordering that callers (heartbeat/brief rendering) are told to expect. A sort on the break event's `ts` (or storing it in the notice) is needed to make the documented contract true.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leasebreak.py:broken_notices

chunk_findings.detail: `_break_idle` marks a broken lease as taken by writing the literal string `"broken"` into `lease.expired_at`. That field is a timestamp in this module (`from .leaseclock import foreign, localize` exists precisely to normalize these `*_at` values), and the lease object keeps living inside the shared `state` for the remainder of the claim. Any consumer that interprets the field as a time — `localize(lease.expired_at)`, a `lease.expired_at > now` liveness comparison, remaining-TTL math, or serializing/rendering `state` (the new yield-requested/broken reporting in brief/doctor/status is exactly this kind of consumer) — gets a `ValueError`/`TypeError` on `"broken"`, or silently loses the break time. Concretely: break an idle lease A, then anything that formats A's expiry from the same snapshot calls `localize("broken")` and blows up; the log event written via `breaking_record` already carries the real break metadata, so the sentinel adds nothing but an unparseable value. If `glob_clash`'s liveness test turns out to compare `expired_at` against `now` rather than testing `is None`, the very next `glob_clash` call in the loop raises inside the claim.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/leases.py:_break_idle (`lease.expired_at = "broken"`)

chunk_findings.detail: The loop performs irreversible side effects (`log.append("lease.expired", …)`, `_remote_drop`, snapshot mutation) for each breakable clash and only afterwards discovers whether the *whole* claim is viable. With two clashing leases — e.g. agent A idle-holds `f` (item X) and agent C actively holds `g` (item Y), both in the claimant's globs, `break_on_timeout=true`, `hold_max_s=600` — `ddflow claim` breaks A first (logging it expired and dropping A's remote claim), then evaluates C, finds it active/not breakable, and returns/raises the clash. The command exits as a failure while A's lease has already been destroyed and B gained nothing; the same happens for `ddflow claim --break` when `asked` is true, where the caller gets a `LeaseError` after other holders' leases were already broken, even though the user's explicit `--break` request was for a lease that could not be broken. Since A's break is only justified as the precursor to the claimant actually taking the item, breaking should be decided (all clashes) before any log/drop mutation, or rolled back on refusal.

chunk_findings.detail: The intent specifies the breaking mechanism as an explicit waiter action: after `hold_max_s` a lease "is breakable by the waiter with `ddflow claim --break`" (and the MCP surface exposes `break` as an opt-in). This new knob defaults to `"true"`, meaning "a claim that meets a breakable lease breaks it by itself". Input: an agent runs a plain `ddflow claim <id>` (no `--break`) for an item whose overlapping lease has a watermark older than `hold_max_s`. Per the decided design it should be refused so the waiter consciously breaks; with this default the ordinary claim silently breaks the lease and parks the holder's lane, so the `--break` flag and the `break` MCP parameter are dead by default and a claimant with no intent to break ends up breaking an idle-but-possibly-working holder. The default should be `false` (or the auto-break behavior should be the exception the design describes), otherwise the stated "breakable" semantics become "auto-broken".

chunk_findings.detail: The `ddflow claim` help adds `--break` with no help string: the snapshot line is bare `--break` followed by a blank line, while every other flag on the command (`--force`, `--queue`, `--resources`, ...) carries a description. Input: a user runs `ddflow claim --help`; the output gives no indication that `--break` breaks a contended, idle lease (work kept) - the only surface that documents it is the MCP tool. Given the intent's requirement that locks be "visible", an undocumented CLI flag defeats part of that goal; the golden snapshot now enshrines the empty help.

chunk_findings.detail: The help text this change adds for `lease.hold_max_s` says: "The holder keeps its branch and worktree and re-claims normally." That describes the pre-amendment design, not the recorded AMENDED behaviour. The change's own intent states (AMENDED 2026-10-15, DX-park-and-resume): "breaking a lease PARKS the holder's lane ... worktree, branch and recorded gates are kept, the restore condition is the waiter's merge, and the holder is restored first when it clears." Under parking, the holder is restored automatically when the waiter merges and does not re-claim; the new text instead tells the holder it must re-claim normally. Concretely: waiter W breaks holder H's lease, W merges, H follows this help text and issues a normal `ddflow claim` — which under the amended design is the wrong action (H should already be restored first; a normal claim can be refused by/compete with other waiters and drops the priority restoration). Either this golden (and the help string it encodes) is stale and the parking behaviour is missing, or it will disagree with an implementation that follows the amendment and the golden test will fail. Either way the added text contradicts the stated design and needs to mention parking/auto-restore.
chunk_findings.title: tests/golden/__snapshots__/test_golden_outputs.ambr (new `lease.hold_max_s` entry)

chunk_findings.detail: The only assertion about the broken holder is that its lease is expired; the comment even claims that an expired lease is what makes "its worktree/branch pointer survive". The AMENDED intent (DX-park-and-resume, 2026-10-15) requires much more: breaking must PARK the holder's lane — worktree, branch and recorded gates kept, the restore condition recorded as *the waiter's merge*, and the holder restored first when that merge clears. An implementation that only stamps `expired_at` (i.e. simply releases the holder, dropping the lane and the restore record — exactly the pre-amendment behaviour) passes every test in this file: nothing after the break checks that T1 is parked, that its worktree/branch association is retained, or that T1 is restored ahead of other claimants once T2 merges. Concrete scenario: merge T2 successfully and then have agent A (or any third agent) claim `src/a.py`; the suite stays green even if T1 was never parked and is not restored first. Given the mandated regression test for the amendment [D-rules-hierarchy], the parking/restore half of the feature is untested.

chunk_findings.detail: The "yield-requested" state is asserted only on the in-process object returned by `LB.judge` (line 57), and the only holder-facing assertion is that a *post-break* heartbeat says "BROKEN" (lines 108-109). Nothing exercises intent item (2) — that the state is *reported* in brief/doctor/status — nor item (3), that the holder sees the request on its next ddflow call while the lease is still intact. Concrete scenario: an implementation where `judge` computes the flag but the renderers (brief/doctor/status) never emit it, so no agent ever learns a waiter wants its files and the lease silently goes from fresh to breakable 60 minutes later; or one where the holder is only told after its lease is already gone. Both pass the entire file, even though the fix's stated purpose is that a pending wait is visible to the holder before the break (B-lease-hold-visibility).

chunk_findings.detail: The new expected `--explain` text describes the superseded design for what happens to the holder: "The holder keeps its branch and worktree and re-claims normally." The change's own AMENDED 2026-10-15 note (DX-park-and-resume) states the opposite lifecycle: breaking a lease PARKS the holder's lane — worktree, branch and recorded gates kept, the restore condition is *the waiter's merge*, and the holder is *restored first when it clears*. As written, an operator reading `ddflow config --explain` is told the holder must win its globs back through an ordinary claim, with no mention of the park, the restore condition, or the restore-first rule; anyone diagnosing a broken lease (or writing the MCP/prompt text from this output) will act on the wrong model, e.g. re-claiming and colliding with the lane that was supposed to be restored to them.

chunk_findings.detail: The intent specifies breaking as an explicit act by the party that was made to wait: "after hold_max_s it is breakable by the waiter with `ddflow claim --break`". The expected output instead introduces `lease.break_on_timeout = True [default]`: "A claim that meets a breakable lease breaks it by itself." With that default, an idle-looking lease is taken away with no decision by anyone — including by a claimant that never recorded a wait (the intent's precondition is a *recorded* wait / a ready item waiting). This also cuts against the posture every other lease knob in this same output states (`reclaim_policy = 'report'` "never steals an expired lease", the deliberate "adoption never breaks an existing repo on day one" defaulting style): the safe behaviour requires configuration, so a holder running a long job that emits no per-item event (the documented progress definition is a commit, gate outcome, note, other item event, or a changed file) can have its lease auto-broken by an unrelated `ddflow claim` after 3600 s.

chunk_findings.detail: The newly added hint block treats "there exists *any* break notice for this item in this agent's history" as "this agent's lease was just taken", and it unconditionally overwrites the accurate hint that the code above it just produced. `LB.broken_notices` accumulates notices per subject across the whole event log (it iterates `events` and returns `list(out.values())`, with no scoping to the agent's current lease cycle — see the previously reported ordering/accumulation problem in that function), and the heartbeat then picks `broken[0]`, i.e. the *oldest* such notice for the item. Concrete input: agent A claims item X at 09:00 and is pre-empted (X broken by a waiter) at 10:00; A re-claims X normally at 11:00, which clears its wait, and the lease then simply expires at 12:00 with no waiter and no break. On A's next `ddflow heartbeat X`, `L.renew` fails → `renewed is False` → `broken` is non-empty because the 10:00 notice is still in the log → `hint` is replaced with the 10:00 break notice, so A is told "the lease was taken from this agent" instead of the correct "; its lease ... has expired -- `claim X` again". Since the whole point of this change is that agents act on what the lease tells them (break → lane parked, restore awaits the waiter's merge, per DX-park-and-resume), this misattribution can make an agent believe another agent is mid-takeover on its files when in fact its own lease merely aged out. The block needs to select the latest notice and only when it corresponds to the lease A just lost (e.g. a notice newer than A's last successful claim/renewal), rather than any historical break for the item.

The plan-then-commit fix only makes the breaks *within* `_break_idle` all-or-nothing; it does nothing about the enclosing `claim`, which still commits every planned break and parks the holder before it can decide it will refuse the claim. Concrete input: agent A's lease on `T1` (globs `g`) has expired; agent B has since claimed `T2` on overlapping `g` and gone idle past `hold_max_s` (and `lease.break_on_timeout` defaults to true, so `asked` is not needed; `force=False` so the new guard `not (force and existing is None)` passes, and `existing` is A's expired lease, i.e. not `None`). chunk_findings.detail: The entry ends the description of a break with "The holder keeps its branch and worktree." and says nothing else about what happens to the holder. The change's own AMENDED 2026-10-15 note (DX-park-and-resume) is explicit that a break PARKS the holder's lane: worktree, branch and recorded gates are kept, the restore condition is the waiter's merge, and the holder is restored first when it clears. Concrete case: agent A's lease on `hot.py` is broken by waiter B; A reads the help text it has (this text), concludes it still owns the item and keeps committing to `ddflow/…`; but the item is parked and its lane is only restored after B merges, so A's commits land on a lane the system treats as unowned (and its stale worktree can be handled by the disposal/sync paths as such). The prior review flagged the older wording here ("…and re-claims normally"); dropping that phrase removes the explicit contradiction with parking, but it does not supply the missing restore contract, so the documented behaviour is still not the implemented behaviour.

chunk_findings.detail:
`claim()` threads the new `broke` list into `_acquire` (so the service can append each lease it actually breaks) but only ever surfaces that list on the success path: it is passed as the last argument to `_claimed`, which attaches it to the success answer (`_claimed(..., broke)` → the `broke=broke` payload). On the refusal path the list is simply thrown away — `claim` returns `early`/the refusal `Outcome` unchanged, and `_acquire`'s own refusal construction (the `except L.LeaseError` branch) also does not include `broke`.

Concrete failure: with `break_on_timeout=true` / `--break`, `ddflow claim <id>` for an item whose globs clash with two leases — one idle/breakable (item X) and one active (item Y) — the service breaks X first (logging `lease.expired` and dropping X's remote claim, both irreversible) and then refuses because Y is active. `claim()` returns the refusal `Outcome`; the `broke` list naming X is discarded, so the caller sees only "refused, Y holds it" and no indication that another agent's lease was destroyed on the way. Because `broke` only reaches `_claimed`, there is no code path in this hunk by which a caller learns of a break that did not end in a successful claim.

This is the API-surface half of the earlier finding #4 (`_break_idle` breaking before viability), and this hunk does not answer it: the diff only adds the `broke` channel to the success `Outcome`, leaving the refusal `Outcome` (both the early-return and the `LeaseError` conversion) without it. Either `broke` must be carried on the refusal `Outcome` as well, or the breaking must be deferred until the whole claim is known viable.

chunk_findings.detail: `broken_notices` promises "newest first" but returns `list(out.values())` with no sort, i.e. the order of each item's *first* break. This slice newly depends on that order: after a holder's lease is taken, a heartbeat for that item filters the notices to the item and takes `broken[0]` — the earliest notice — and overwrites `hint` with it. Input: agent A holds item X, X is broken at t=100, A re-claims and is broken again at t=200; A then calls `ddflow heartbeat X`. `broken` is built oldest-first, so `broken[0]` is the t=100 notice and A is shown the stale break (with the docstring's implied "most recent" contract violated). Because the notice is deduped per item, A never sees the t=200 break at all. The diff adds no sort and no change to `broken_notices`, so the fix does not answer this finding.

chunk_findings.detail: The AMENDED 2026-10-15 design (DX-park-and-resume) says that breaking a lease PARKS the holder's lane: worktree, branch and recorded gates are kept, the restore condition is *the waiter's merge*, and the holder is *restored first* when that merges clears. This file is the only place the break is produced and announced, and it implements the pre-amendment "release and re-claim" lifecycle instead. Lines 17-18 say "the holder re-claims through the normal door"; `notice_text` line 179 tells the holder "`ddflow claim {item}` takes it back once the files are free"; and `breaking_record` (134-144) writes only the ordinary expiry fields plus `broken_by`/`broken_for`/`idle_s`/`files` - nothing marks the holder as parked and no restore condition/restore-first contract is carried for any reader. Concrete failure: agent A holds T1, B runs `ddflow claim T1 --break` after `hold_max_s`; on A's next `ddflow` call/heartbeat `notice_text` instructs A to re-claim the item rather than telling A it is parked, and no consumer of the `lease.expired` payload can know that A must be restored ahead of everyone else once B's merge lands. The earlier findings on this design mismatch were about the `--explain` help text, the golden snapshots/transcript and the regression test; none of them covers this runtime notice/payload, so fixing the help strings would leave A being sent to fight B for the globs.

chunk_findings.detail: The earlier "loop breaks before knowing the claim can succeed" finding is only answered *inside* `_break_idle`: decisions are now batched, but the durable side effects (`log.append("lease.expired", …)`, `_remote_drop`, and the resulting in-state expiry) are still written before `claim()` has finished its own refusals. The very next block after the call site is the unchanged "Taking over an EXPIRED lease … needs `--force` for the expiry alone" check, and admission (`resource_shortfall`, the `offer` refusal) also raises later. Concrete input: agent A idle-holds glob `f` on item X with no progress past `hold_max_s`; the claimant claims item Y (globs overlap `f`) whose own lease record is an expired one left by a crashed agent C, and passes no `--force`, with `break_on_timeout=true`. `_break_idle` plans A, sets `A.lease.expired_at = stamp`, logs `lease.expired` for A and drops A's remote claim, returns None; then the expiry/force check immediately raises `LeaseError` telling the claimant to use `--force`. A's live lease and remote claim were destroyed although nothing was claimed and no break was ever justified by the claimant's success. Moving the write loop after the configure-check only covers the *clash* dimension; the claim as a whole can still fail after the break has become irreversible in the log.

chunk_findings.detail: Both the "later clash is not breakable" path and the `except LeaseError` path revert planned leases with `held.expired_at = ""` instead of restoring the value they overwrote. That field is a timestamp in this module (`from .leaseclock import foreign, localize` exists to normalise these `*_at` values), and a contended *live* lease is exactly one whose `expired_at` is a real expiry (the heartbeat "renews an idle lease", i.e. pushes the expiry forward) — otherwise setting `lease.expired_at = stamp` would not be the way to make `glob_clash` stop seeing it live in the first place. Concrete input: A idle-holds `f` (breakable), C actively holds `g` (not breakable), the claimant's globs cover both, `break_on_timeout=true` and no `--break`. The loop plans A (overwriting A's real future expiry with `stamp`), reaches C, and rolls A back to `""`; the refused claim leaves A holding a lease whose `expired_at` is no longer the expiry it had, so any `localize(lease.expired_at)`/TTL/liveness computation on it (or on the reloaded state) is now wrong — e.g. it can read as epoch-0/expired, letting the next claim take A's globs without waiting for `hold_max_s`. The earlier finding about writing a non-timestamp (`"broken"`) into this field is therefore only answered for the success path; the abort paths reintroduce the same defect, and they do so on a claim that is being *refused*, which should have left the holder's lease untouched.

chunk_findings.detail: The break notice is the only runtime surface for a break, and it describes the superseded (pre-amendment) lifecycle: "Its branch and worktree are kept and {b['holder']} is told." The change's own AMENDED 2026-10-15 note (DX-park-and-resume) requires that breaking **parks** the holder's lane — branch, worktree *and recorded gates* kept, the restore condition recorded as *the waiter's merge*, and the holder restored first when that merge clears. The message therefore cannot distinguish a parked lane from a merely expired lease, exactly the ambiguity the amendment was written to remove. chunk_findings.detail: The new knob defaults to `"true"`, i.e. "a claim that meets a breakable lease breaks it by itself". The decided design (bullets (2) and (3) of the intent) makes breaking an explicit act by the party that was made to wait on a *recorded* wait: after `hold_max_s` the lease "is breakable by the waiter with `ddflow claim --break`", and the holder is supposed to see the yield request on its next call. With this default, a plain `ddflow claim <id>` that merely overlaps an idle-looking lease takes it away with no `--break`, no recorded waiter, and before the holder has had any chance to react — exactly the runaway-liveness condition the item was filed to stop. The earlier finding on this same file is still open (untriaged) and nothing in this diff answers it: the template still ships `new = "true"`, and the paired snapshot changes in `tests/golden/__snapshots__/test_golden_mcp_tools.ambr` even hard-code the contradiction, since `ddflow_claim`'s description continues to promise "Refuses (exit 3) if another agent holds it or an overlapping item" while the same tool now advertises a `break` property and the default silently breaks instead of refusing. chunk_findings.detail: `last_activity` returns `0.0` for any "no evidence of work" path (missing/unreadable tree, failed `git status`, failed `git log`), and `last_commit_at` returns `0.0` whenever `base` or `branch` is falsy. `0.0` is epoch 1970-01-01, not a neutral sentinel, so the consumer described in this same change (`services.leasebreak`, comparing `now - watermark` against `idle_max_s`/`hold_max_s`) sees an *infinitely old* watermark. Input: a holder whose worktree was moved or whose `git log` fails to run (e.g. a broken `PATH`/dubious-ownership repo) returns `0.0`, so an actively-working lease is judged idle, marked yield-requested, and becomes breakable by a waiter. Nothing in the reviewed diff changes this function or its callers.

chunk_findings.detail: The docstring promises "newest first", but the body iterates `events` in log order, writes into a plain dict keyed by subject, and returns `list(out.values())` — insertion order, i.e. oldest break first; overwriting `out[e.subject]` on a later break does not move the key. Input: an agent's lease on `a` is broken at 10:00, re-claimed, broken again at 12:00, while `b` is broken at 11:00; the returned list is `[a(12:00), b(11:00)]` — the oldest-first order the docstring forbids (and `a` sorts at its first break position even if you fixed the dict). The reviewed diff does not touch this function.

chunk_findings.detail: `_break_idle` breaks leases one at a time inside `while clash:` and commits each break (`log.append("lease.expired", ...)`, `_remote_drop`, parking the holder per DX-park-and-resume) before judging the *next* clash. If a later clashing lease is not breakable while `asked`/`break_on_timeout` is in effect, the function raises `LeaseError` (or `return clash` when not asked) after already having broken and parked the earlier holder; the enclosing `claim` then fails, so the waiter gets no lease but a holder has still been evicted and parked. Nothing in the reviewed diff changes this loop.

chunk_findings.detail: The shipped default is `true` (confirmed by the reviewed README row `| \`lease.break_on_timeout\` | \`true\` |  |`). The intent specifies an explicit, attributable act: "after hold_max_s it is breakable by the waiter with `ddflow claim --break`", gated by a recorded wait (DX-lease-wait-cycle). With this default a plain `ddflow claim` auto-breaks any contended lease past `hold_max_s` with a stale watermark, so the `--break` flag and the recorded-wait gate are inert. Input: agent B runs `ddflow claim T2` (no `--break`, no recorded wait) while A holds T2 with an idle watermark past both timeouts — A is evicted without ever being marked and seen as yield-requested. chunk_findings.detail: `claim()` now allocates `broke: list = []`, threads it through `_acquire(... {"break_lease": break_lease, "broke": broke})` into `L.acquire`, and only surfaces it in the success answer via `_claimed(..., broke)`. On the refusal path it returns `lz` (the `Outcome`) directly, so the `broke` list is dropped. This matters because `L.acquire` can break (and, per the AMENDED note, park) one clashing holder and only afterwards fail on a later clash: the prior finding on `services/leases._break_idle` (breaking one lease at a time inside `while clash:`, committing `lease.expired`/`_remote_drop`/parking before re-examining the next clash) is still untriaged, and nothing in this hunk changes it. Concrete case: waiter runs `ddflow claim T3 --break`; T1 is an idle, breakable holder of a contested glob and T2 is an active, non-breakable holder of another contested glob. `_break_idle` breaks T1 and parks its lane, then raises `LeaseError` for T2; `_acquire` catches it and returns an `Outcome`, and this line returns that refusal immediately — `broke` (already containing T1's break) never reaches the caller, so the CLI reports only "refused" while T1 has in fact been broken and parked. The new `broke` reporting field is therefore inert in the one case (partial break + refusal) where the waiter most needs it. This is the same defect the earlier review raised; it still holds because this hunk adds no handling on the `isinstance(lz, O.Outcome)` branch and the author's triage is `untriaged`.

chunk_findings.detail: The newly added hint block treats "there exists *any* break notice for this item in this agent's history" as "this agent's lease was just taken", and it unconditionally overwrites the accurate hint that the code above it just produced. `LB.broken_notices` accumulates notices per subject across the whole event log (it iterates `events` and returns `list(out.values())`, with no scoping to the agent's current lease cycle — see the previously reported ordering/accumulation problem in that function), and the heartbeat then picks `broken[0]`, i.e. the *oldest* such notice for the item. Concrete input: agent A claims item X at 09:00 and is pre-empted (X broken by a waiter) at 10:00; A re-claims X normally at 11:00, which clears its wait, and the lease then simply expires at 12:00 with no waiter and no break. On A's next `ddflow heartbeat X`, `L.renew` fails → `renewed is False` → `broken` is non-empty because the 10:00 notice is still in the log → `hint` is replaced with the 10:00 break notice, so A is told "the lease was taken from this agent" instead of the correct "; its lease ... has expired -- `claim X` again". Since the whole point of this change is that agents act on what the lease tells them (break → lane parked, restore awaits the waiter's merge, per DX-park-and-resume), this misattribution can make an agent believe another agent is mid-takeover on its files when in fact its own lease merely aged out. The block needs to select the latest notice and only when it corresponds to the lease A just lost (e.g. a notice newer than A's last successful claim/renewal), rather than any historical break for the item.

chunk_findings.detail: The progress watermark collapses "unknown" into epoch. `last_commit_at` returns `0.0` whenever `base` or `branch` is falsy, and also when `git log base..branch` fails or prints nothing (`base` ref not fetched locally, shallow clone, or the holder's commits already contained in `base`); `last_change_at` returns `0.0` for a clean tree and whenever `git status` fails — e.g. a concurrent git process holds `.git/index.lock`, which is routine with several agents on one repo. If the commit probe is empty and the tree is clean (exactly an agent that committed everything and is now waiting on a gate), `last_activity` returns `0.0`, i.e. 1970-01-01; the caller described in this change compares `now - watermark` against `idle_max_s`/`hold_max_s`, so ~56 years of "idleness" is reported and a contended lease held by a working agent is marked yield-requested and then broken after `hold_max_s`. The earlier finding on this file is not answered: the docstring calls `0.0` "no evidence", but the returned value is an ordinary timestamp with no distinct "unknown" state.

chunk_findings.detail: The user-facing story this file tells is the pre-amendment one and contradicts the change's own AMENDED 2026-10-15 decision (DX-park-and-resume). The module docstring says breaking is harmless because "Nothing is deleted -- the lease object keeps its worktree and branch, **the holder re-claims through the normal door**", and `notice_text` — which `broken_notices` supplies "for the holder's heartbeat and brief" — tells the broken agent: "Your branch X and worktree Y are kept. `ddflow claim <item>` takes it back once the files are free." The amendment deliberately replaced that mechanism: a break PARKS the holder's lane, the restore condition is the waiter's merge, and the holder is restored first when it clears. Concretely: agent A holds `hot.py`, agent B breaks it (B's claim records the `lease.expired` with `broken_by`), and A's next `ddflow` call prints the notice above. Per the recorded decision A's lane is parked and is restored automatically once B merges; A following the notice and running `ddflow claim hot.py` is exactly the pre-amendment behaviour the amendment removed, and the module docstring that callers/readers see asserts the same stale semantics. The same wording problem was already flagged for the template/transcript help text (findings 6/10/11); this is the source-of-truth surface that generated those strings, and it is not answered by any change here — the amendment's parking/restore-first semantics are simply not described.

chunk_findings.detail: `_break_idle` is invoked *before* the claim's own "taking over an EXPIRED lease needs `--force`" check (the unchanged block immediately below the insertion, whose comment is visible in the diff: "Taking over an EXPIRED lease ... needs `--force` for the expiry alone. It must not also waive the overlap check: expiry freed those files, and a live lease granted on them since stands (B08b6e40bfb)"). The plan-then-commit fix only makes the breaks *within* `_break_idle` all-or-nothing; it does nothing about the enclosing `claim`, which still commits every planned break and parks the holder before it can decide it will refuse the claim. Concrete input: agent A's lease on `T1` (globs `g`) has expired; agent B has since claimed `T2` on overlapping `g` and gone idle past `hold_max_s` (and `lease.break_on_timeout` defaults to true, so `asked` is not needed; `force=False` so the new guard `not (force and existing is None)` passes, and `existing` is A's expired lease, i.e. not `None`). A runs `ddflow claim T1` without `--force`. `_break_idle` plans B as breakable, sets `lease.expired_at`, and then commits `lease.expired`, `_remote_drop` and B's lane parking (DX-park-and-resume) — and only then does the surrounding expiry check raise, since the item's own lease is expired and `--force` was not given. Result: B's live lease is broken and B's lane is parked for a claim that is refused, i.e. exactly the "a live lease granted on them since stands" invariant the same code block documents is broken. The same ordering also means the `broke` out-parameter is populated before the failure, so the API can print "BROKE <item>" to a claimant that did not get the item.

chunk_findings.detail: The only user-facing description of what `--break` does, added here, still describes the pre-amendment contract: `help="Break a contended, idle lease (work kept)."`, `cli_help="break a contended lease idle for [lease].hold_max_s (its work is kept)"`, and the breaker's own confirmation text `"Its branch and worktree are kept and {b['holder']} is told."`. This change's own AMENDED 2026-10-15 decision (DX-park-and-resume) states that breaking PARKS the holder's lane: the worktree, branch and recorded gates are kept, **the restore condition is the waiter's merge**, and the holder is restored first when it clears. Concretely: agent B runs `ddflow claim T2 --break` and reads `BROKE T1's lease (...). Its branch and worktree are kept and A is told.` — nothing tells B that T1's lane is now parked rather than merely "kept", nor that B's own merge is the trigger that restores A. A user (or an MCP agent reading the tool schema, since the same string is the param description) is left with the pre-amendment mental model — holder keeps its work and effectively continues/re-claims — which is exactly the misstatement reported earlier for `lease.hold_max_s` in the golden snapshot and the setup transcript; this hunk introduces the same wording into the CLI/param surfaces instead of correcting it while the amended mechanism is being wired in. chunk_findings.detail:
`claim()` threads the new `broke` list into `_acquire` (so the service can append each lease it actually breaks) but only ever surfaces that list on the success path: it is passed as the last argument to `_claimed`, which attaches it to the success answer (`_claimed(..., broke)` → the `broke=broke` payload). On the refusal path the list is simply thrown away — `claim` returns `early`/the refusal `Outcome` unchanged, and `_acquire`'s own refusal construction (the `except L.LeaseError` branch) also does not include `broke`.

Concrete failure: with `break_on_timeout=true` / `--break`, `ddflow claim <id>` for an item whose globs clash with two leases — one idle/breakable (item X) and one active (item Y) — the service breaks X first (logging `lease.expired` and dropping X's remote claim, both irreversible) and then refuses because Y is active. `claim()` returns the refusal `Outcome`; the `broke` list naming X is discarded, so the caller sees only "refused, Y holds it" and no indication that another agent's lease was destroyed on the way. Because `broke` only reaches `_claimed`, there is no code path in this hunk by which a caller learns of a break that did not end in a successful claim.

This is the API-surface half of the earlier finding #4 (`_break_idle` breaking before viability), and this hunk does not answer it: the diff only adds the `broke` channel to the success `Outcome`, leaving the refusal `Outcome` (both the early-return and the `LeaseError` conversion) without it. Either `broke` must be carried on the refusal `Outcome` as well, or the breaking must be deferred until the whole claim is known viable.

chunk_findings.detail: `broken_notices` promises "newest first" but returns `list(out.values())` with no sort, i.e. the order of each item's *first* break. This slice newly depends on that order: after a holder's lease is taken, a heartbeat for that item filters the notices to the item and takes `broken[0]` — the earliest notice — and overwrites `hint` with it. Input: agent A holds item X, X is broken at t=100, A re-claims and is broken again at t=200; A then calls `ddflow heartbeat X`. `broken` is built oldest-first, so `broken[0]` is the t=100 notice and A is shown the stale break (with the docstring's implied "most recent" contract violated). Because the notice is deduped per item, A never sees the t=200 break at all. The diff adds no sort and no change to `broken_notices`, so the fix does not answer this finding.

chunk_findings.detail: The AMENDED 2026-10-15 design (DX-park-and-resume) says that breaking a lease PARKS the holder's lane: worktree, branch and recorded gates are kept, the restore condition is *the waiter's merge*, and the holder is *restored first* when that merges clears. This file is the only place the break is produced and announced, and it implements the pre-amendment "release and re-claim" lifecycle instead. Lines 17-18 say "the holder re-claims through the normal door"; `notice_text` line 179 tells the holder "`ddflow claim {item}` takes it back once the files are free"; and `breaking_record` (134-144) writes only the ordinary expiry fields plus `broken_by`/`broken_for`/`idle_s`/`files` - nothing marks the holder as parked and no restore condition/restore-first contract is carried for any reader. Concrete failure: agent A holds T1, B runs `ddflow claim T1 --break` after `hold_max_s`; on A's next `ddflow` call/heartbeat `notice_text` instructs A to re-claim the item rather than telling A it is parked, and no consumer of the `lease.expired` payload can know that A must be restored ahead of everyone else once B's merge lands. chunk_findings.detail: The earlier "loop breaks before knowing the claim can succeed" finding is only answered *inside* `_break_idle`: decisions are now batched, but the durable side effects (`log.append("lease.expired", …)`, `_remote_drop`, and the resulting in-state expiry) are still written before `claim()` has finished its own refusals. The very next block after the call site is the unchanged "Taking over an EXPIRED lease … needs `--force` for the expiry alone" check, and admission (`resource_shortfall`, the `offer` refusal) also raises later. Concrete input: agent A idle-holds glob `f` on item X with no progress past `hold_max_s`; the claimant claims item Y (globs overlap `f`) whose own lease record is an expired one left by a crashed agent C, and passes no `--force`, with `break_on_timeout=true`. `_break_idle` plans A, sets `A.lease.expired_at = stamp`, logs `lease.expired` for A and drops A's remote claim, returns None; then the expiry/force check immediately raises `LeaseError` telling the claimant to use `--force`. A's live lease and remote claim were destroyed although nothing was claimed and no break was ever justified by the claimant's success. Moving the write loop after the configure-check only covers the *clash* dimension; the claim as a whole can still fail after the break has become irreversible in the log.

chunk_findings.detail: Both the "later clash is not breakable" path and the `except LeaseError` path revert planned leases with `held.expired_at = ""` instead of restoring the value they overwrote. That field is a timestamp in this module (`from .leaseclock import foreign, localize` exists to normalise these `*_at` values), and a contended *live* lease is exactly one whose `expired_at` is a real expiry (the heartbeat "renews an idle lease", i.e. pushes the expiry forward) — otherwise setting `lease.expired_at = stamp` would not be the way to make `glob_clash` stop seeing it live in the first place. Concrete input: A idle-holds `f` (breakable), C actively holds `g` (not breakable), the claimant's globs cover both, `break_on_timeout=true` and no `--break`. The loop plans A (overwriting A's real future expiry with `stamp`), reaches C, and rolls A back to `""`; the refused claim leaves A holding a lease whose `expired_at` is no longer the expiry it had, so any `localize(lease.expired_at)`/TTL/liveness computation on it (or on the reloaded state) is now wrong — e.g. it can read as epoch-0/expired, letting the next claim take A's globs without waiting for `hold_max_s`. The earlier finding about writing a non-timestamp (`"broken"`) into this field is therefore only answered for the success path; the abort paths reintroduce the same defect, and they do so on a claim that is being *refused*, which should have left the holder's lease untouched.

chunk_findings.detail: The break notice is the only runtime surface for a break, and it describes the superseded (pre-amendment) lifecycle: "Its branch and worktree are kept and {b['holder']} is told." The change's own AMENDED 2026-10-15 note (DX-park-and-resume) requires that breaking **parks** the holder's lane — branch, worktree *and recorded gates* kept, the restore condition recorded as *the waiter's merge*, and the holder restored first when that merge clears. Concrete input: a claimant runs `ddflow claim <id> --break`, the holder's lane is parked, and the claimant (and any operator reading the transcript) is told only that the holder "keeps its branch and worktree and is told", i.e. that it will resume on its own — which is false under the design being built. The message therefore cannot distinguish a parked lane from a merely expired lease, exactly the ambiguity the amendment was written to remove. (Same wording defect previously flagged for the config/help text, but here it is the runtime output the waiter actually sees.)
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/lifecycle_cli.py:252 (`claim_text`, `broke` loop)

chunk_findings.detail:
The notice asserts a wait unconditionally, but the code path shown forwards only `break_lease=bool(a.get("break"))`; nothing in the diff shows that a *recorded* wait (DX-lease-wait-cycle, the intent's precondition for breakability) is required before the break fires. Given `break_on_timeout` exists as a knob, a plain `ddflow claim` for an overlapping item whose watermark is old can reach this same message, and the claimant is then told it "waited" for a lease it never queued on. Under the intent ("a lease that another ready item is waiting on (a recorded wait) … is breakable"), breaking without a recorded wait is out of contract, and the message makes that indistinguishable from the legitimate case.

I did not re-report the earlier numbered findings: the files they target (treeactivity, leasebreak notices, `_break_idle`, the config template and transcript snapshots, the tests) are not part of the diff shown to me, so I cannot confirm or refute them from this part.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/lifecycle_cli.py:255 ("no progress for {…}s while you waited")

chunk_findings.detail: The new knob defaults to `"true"`, i.e. "a claim that meets a breakable lease breaks it by itself". The decided design (bullets (2) and (3) of the intent) makes breaking an explicit act by the party that was made to wait on a *recorded* wait: after `hold_max_s` the lease "is breakable by the waiter with `ddflow claim --break`", and the holder is supposed to see the yield request on its next call. With this default, a plain `ddflow claim <id>` that merely overlaps an idle-looking lease takes it away with no `--break`, no recorded waiter, and before the holder has had any chance to react — exactly the runaway-liveness condition the item was filed to stop. The earlier finding on this same file is still open (untriaged) and nothing in this diff answers it: the template still ships `new = "true"`, and the paired snapshot changes in `tests/golden/__snapshots__/test_golden_mcp_tools.ambr` even hard-code the contradiction, since `ddflow_claim`'s description continues to promise "Refuses (exit 3) if another agent holds it or an overlapping item" while the same tool now advertises a `break` property and the default silently breaks instead of refusing. Input: agent runs `ddflow claim X` with `--globs f`, agent C sits on an overlapping glob with a watermark older than `hold_max_s` but a live heartbeat; expected refusal (or a waiter-gated break), actual: C's lease is expired and its lane parked with no `--break` and no recorded wait.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/upgrade/unreleased/knob_added.lease.break_on_timeout.toml

chunk_findings.detail: The intent states breaking is an explicit act by the party that was made to wait: after `hold_max_s` a lease "is breakable by the waiter with `ddflow claim --break`", and the precondition is a *recorded* wait (DX-lease-wait-cycle). This hunk ships two things that contradict that. (a) `lease.break_on_timeout = True [default]` with the text "A claim that meets a breakable lease breaks it by itself" means an ordinary `ddflow claim <id>` (no `--break`) seizes the lease with no decision by the waiter; the matching prior finding (#11) is untriaged and nothing here changes it — the text is verbatim the superseded default. (b) `lease.idle_max_s` defines contention as "a recorded wait, **or a claim of an overlapping file**", widening "another ready item is waiting on it (a recorded wait)" into any overlapping claimant. Concrete input: agent B runs plain `ddflow claim T1` while B has recorded no wait and merely touches an overlapping glob; T1's holder has been idle past `hold_max_s`; B's claim breaks T1's lease although no wait was ever recorded and nobody opted in.
chunk_findings.title: tests/golden/__snapshots__/test_golden_outputs.ambr (`lease.break_on_timeout = True [default]` + `lease.idle_max_s` contention clause)

chunk_findings.detail: The intent item (2) requires the yield-requested state to be "marked yield-requested in brief/doctor/status", yet this new user-facing documentation enumerates the surfaces as "in the holder's heartbeat and in brief" only — doctor and status are dropped, and "heartbeat" (a renewal response, intent item 3) is substituted for them. Input: a coordinator (not the holder) runs `ddflow doctor` or `ddflow status` on the contended item; per the documented behaviour neither surface shows that the lease has been yield-requested, so the "hot-file locks are visible" requirement of D-lease-hold-limit is only met for the holder, not for anyone deciding whether to break.
chunk_findings.title: tests/golden/__snapshots__/test_golden_outputs.ambr (`lease.idle_max_s` help text)

chunk_findings.detail: Prior finding 8 still holds, and the visible test is the proof. The only assertion the change makes about the broken holder is `assert st.items["T1"].lease.expired_at`, annotated "kept, expired: its worktree/branch pointer survives" — i.e. exactly the pre-amendment model ("the holder re-claims normally"). The recorded AMENDED intent (DX-park-and-resume, 2026-10-15) requires breaking to PARK the holder's lane: worktree, branch and recorded gates kept, the restore condition recorded as *the waiter's merge*, and the holder restored first when that merge clears. Nothing in the diff asserts a park record, a restore condition, or resumption of T1 after T2 merges, so an implementation that only stamps `expired_at` (and lets A re-claim from scratch) passes the entire suite. The fix/probe does not answer the finding: `test_a_claim_that_cannot_break_everything_breaks_nothing` (line 157) also only checks `expired_at`, and no test ever inspects the holder's worktree/branch/gate state after a break.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lease_progress_breakable.py:104

chunk_findings.detail: Prior findings 5 and 11 still hold, and this diff encodes them. `test_claim_breaks_a_heartbeat_only_lease_and_tells_both_agents` calls `run_cli(repo, "claim", "T2", "--no-worktree", agent=B)` — no `--break` — after `_setup`, which never touches `lease.break_on_timeout`, and then asserts `code == 0 and "BROKE T1" in out`. The decided mechanism is explicit: after `hold_max_s` the lease "is breakable by the waiter with `ddflow claim --break`" (the MCP surface likewise exposes `break` as opt-in). With this test as written the default is auto-break: any plain `ddflow claim <id>` whose overlapping lease is idle silently takes the lease and drops the holder's remote claim, with no `--break` decision by anyone, so an implementation that never requires the flag stays green. The companion test (`test_break_flag_is_required_when_break_on_timeout_is_off`, line 128) confirms the flag is only required when the knob is turned off, i.e. the contradiction is in the default, not in the flag plumbing.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lease_progress_breakable.py:100

chunk_findings.detail: Intent item (2) requires the lease to be "marked yield-requested in brief/doctor/status". The change verifies only `brief` ("Yield requested" in out, line 146) and the holder-facing heartbeat (line 144). The other two promised surfaces — `doctor` and `status` — are never invoked anywhere in the file, so a regression that stops rendering the yield request in `ddflow status`/`ddflow doctor` (the surfaces an operator or a second agent is most likely to read before deciding to wait) passes the suite. Concrete input: run `ddflow status` while T1 is yield-requested; nothing in this diff would fail if it printed no marker.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lease_progress_breakable.py:145

chunk_findings.detail: The `--explain` text this change adds for `lease.break_on_timeout` says `"A claim that meets a breakable lease breaks it by itself. Off: the claimant must say so (ddflow claim --break)"`, and the entry is listed as a `default` with value `true`. The decided intent for this item specifies the mechanism as an explicit act by the party that was made to wait — after `hold_max_s` a contended lease "is breakable by the waiter with `ddflow claim --break`" — and makes the break conditional on a *recorded* wait (`idle_max_s` is defined over "a lease that another agent waits for"). With this default, a plain `ddflow claim <id>` (no `--break`) made by an agent that never recorded a wait silently takes an idle-looking lease away from its holder, so the opt-in `--break` path is never the one exercised and no person or coordinator decides the break. The triage on this finding is `untriaged`, and the hunk still carries the same text and the same `true` default, so nothing in the diff answers it; the corresponding knob defaults in `ddflow/templates/upgrade/unreleased/knob_added.lease.break_on_timeout.toml` and `tests/golden/__snapshots__/test_golden_outputs.ambr` are unchanged in this part, so this expected output continues to describe superseding behaviour.

chunk_findings.detail: The snapshot this change adds declares the new knob with the default `True` and the text "A claim that meets a breakable lease breaks it by itself." The recorded decision for this knob (the intent's `D-lease-hold-limit`) makes the break the *waiter's* explicit act: "after hold_max_s it is breakable by the waiter with `ddflow claim --break`". Concrete failure: agent A idles on item `X` holding `f`; agent B runs a plain `ddflow claim Y` (no `--break`) whose globs include `f`. With `True [default]` the claim silently expires A's lease, drops A's claim ref and takes the files, with no decision by the party that was made to wait — and, per the same help text, even without that waiter ever having recorded a wait for those globs. The earlier finding's fix/probe does not answer this: the diff still ships `True [default]` and the "breaks it by itself" wording, so the opt-in `--break` the decision specifies is not the default path. [D-lease-hold-limit]

chunk_findings.detail:
The expected `--explain` text still ends the lifecycle at "The holder keeps its branch and worktree." and never states the recorded AMENDED behaviour (`DX-park-and-resume`): breaking PARKS the holder's lane — worktree, branch **and recorded gates** kept, the restore condition is **the waiter's merge**, and the holder is **restored first when it clears**. The edit dropped the earlier "and re-claims normally" clause, but dropping that clause is not the missing fix: an operator who reads `ddflow config --explain` and then breaks a contended lease still has no signal that the holder's module is parked and cannot proceed on those globs until the waiter merges, which is exactly the "locks must be visible" property this change exists to provide. [DX-park-and-resume] [D-lease-hold-limit]

chunk_findings.detail: The new `lease.hold_max_s` text says a contended idle lease is broken and "recorded as a lease.expired event", while the neighbouring `lease.reclaim_policy` entry, two lines later in the same output, documents the default as "'report' … never steals an expired lease — it names the worktree so a human can rescue in-flight work." Read together, the same `--explain` output promises both that an expired (broken) lease is taken by the waiter and that an expired lease is never taken. Since the two paths share the `lease.expired` event, the docs give no precedence, so an operator cannot tell from the output whether the default break is allowed to override the default "never steal" policy.

Compute the watermarks of the leases the claim overlaps before taking the lock (and re-verify under it with the lock-free fold), per the decide_then_append contract. Found by the standards review (roborev) of DX-lease-progress-breakable. Regression test: a claim --break holds the lock for no git subprocess.
